abstract:
Cancer is a systemic disease continuously monitored and
responded
to by the human global immune system. Peripheral blood immune cells,
integral to this surveillance, exhibit variable phenotypes during
tumor progression. Glycosylation, as one of the most prevalent and
significant post-translational modifications of proteins, plays a
crucial role in immune system recognition and response. Glycan analysis
has become a key method for biomarker discovery. LacNAc, a prominent
glycosylation modification, regulates immune cell activity and function.
Therefore, we applied our previously developed single-cell glycomic
multiomics to analyze peripheral blood in cancer patients. This platform
utilizes chemoenzymatic labeling with DNA barcodes for detecting and
quantifying LacNAc levels at single-cell resolution without altering
the transcriptional status of immune cells. For the first time, we
systematically integrated single-cell transcriptome, T cell receptor
(TCR) repertoire, and glycan epitope LacNAc analyses in tumor-patient-derived
peripheral blood. Our integrated analysis reveals that lower-stage
bladder cancer patients showed significantly higher levels of LacNAc
in peripheral T cells, and peripheral T cells with high levels of
cell-surface LacNAc exhibit higher cytotoxicity and TCR clonal expansion.
In summary, we identified LacNAc as a potential cell-surface effector
marker for peripheral T cells in bladder cancer patients, which enhances
our understanding of peripheral immune cells and offers potential
advancements in liquid biopsy.
methods:
Method and Materials
Patients
This study included 5 BC patients at Nanjing
Drum Tower Hospital (Nanjing, China) from August 2015 to April 2022.
The pathological data of 5 patients with prognostic information are
recorded in
Table S1
. This study was approved
by the Ethics Committee of Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital (2021–394–01).
GDP-Fucose-ssDNA Synthesis and Labeling
The GDP-Fucose-ssDNA
synthesis process is consistent with our previous work.
17
In brief, GDP-Fucose-Am was produced from GDP-Fucose-Azide
using Pd/C in MeOH/ddH2O. GDP-Fucose-Am was then added to NaHCO
3
, THF, and NHS-PEG4-Tz (Click Chemistry Tools) to create GDP-Fucose-Am-Tz.
TCO-ssDNA was synthesized by reacting NH
2
-ssDNA (Sangon
Co., Ltd., Shanghai.) and NHS-PEG
4
-TCO (Xi’an Confluore
Biological Technology Co., Ltd.) in Borate Buffered Saline solution
with DMSO for 2 h at final concentrations of 200 μM and 8 mM,
respectively. TCO-ssDNA was purified using DNA adsorption columns
(Baiaolaibo Co., Ltd., Beijing). Finally, GDP-Fucose-Am-Tz and TCO-ssDNA
underwent a click reaction in a 1:1 ratio to synthesize GDP-Fucose-ssDNA.
To ensure compatibility with the Singleron platform, the probe was
designed as follows: TGTCAAGATGCTACCGTTCAGAGTAAGAGCCCGGCAAGAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA*A*A.
Cells were resuspended in 1× PBS containing 50 μg/mL
FucT, 20 mM Mg
2+
, 0.1 mg mL
–1
salmon
testes DNA, 0.1 μM Cy5-(dT)
25
, and 20 μM GDP-Fucose-ssDNA.
Following the completion of GDP-Fucose-ssDNA labeling, the detection
was carried out using an Agilent NovoCyte Quanteon flow cytometer.
Flow Cytometry
The PBMC fraction was isolated from
peripheral blood by Ficoll-Paque density gradient separation and then
prepared as single-cell suspensions, and Fc receptors were blocked
with Human TruStain FcX (Biolegend, 422302) before staining with fluorescent
antibodies. A Zombie Aqua Fixable Viability Kit was used to distinguish
live/dead cells (Biolegend, 423102). Alexa Flour700-antihuman-CD45
was used to identify immune cells, and the gating strategy is shown
in
Figure S1A
. The labeling of LacNAc (GDP-Fucose-ssDNA)
was tested with APC-poly(dT)-Cy5, as shown in
Figure S1B
.
Single-Cell Library Production
Single-cell suspensions
were captured using the microfluidic chip, and we used the Singleron
single-cell RNA-seq approach (GEXSCOPE Single-Cell RNA-seq Kit, Singleron
Biotechnologies, Nanjing, China), coupled with LacNAc-seq and scTCR-seq,
allowing for the simultaneous detection of the single-cell transcriptome,
LacNAc, and TCR clonotypes of PBMCs from bladder cancer patients.
Our group previously developed LacNAcTag ssDNA sequences, which can
be found in the previous article for details.
17
The poly(A) tail of mRNAs, TCR region, and LacNAc of cells were
captured by magnetic beads. In short, single-cell isolation, lysis,
reverse transcription, and complementary DNA (cDNA) amplification
were conducted based on the protocol. The construction of libraries
for mRNA, LacNAcTags, and TCR was carried out using Singleron RNA-seq
with feature barcoding and scTCR-seq protocols. Sequencing of the
libraries was conducted using the Illumina HiSeq X platform (Illumina).
Single-Cell Data Generation
Total reads from FASTQ
files were processed to generate gene expression matrices by the Singleron
platform CeleScope (
https://github.com/singleron-RD/CeleScope
). We filtered invalid reads and then extracted cell barcodes and
unique molecular identifiers (UMI). Prior to the mapping of reads
to GRCh38, reads with poly(A) tails were trimmed. Subsequently, we
grouped the same cell barcode, UMI, and gene to generate the number
of UMIs per gene per cell.
The analysis of LacNAcTags was also
performed using the Singleron platform CeleScope (multitag module)
for UMI counting. Normalized analysis of LacNAc was performed using
the following formula:
X
i
= log (
C
i
+ 1).
X
i
represented
log normalized data of the LacNAc and
C
i
represented the original UMI counts. The TCR repertoire data generated
from the flv_trust4 assay within CeleScope, the scRepertoire R package
was utilized for detailed analysis. The subsequent analysis was supported
by Seurat packages in R. The combination of the transcriptome, TCR,
and LacNAc was initially created into one Seurat object.
Quality Control and the Cell Type Annotation
The Seurat
package within R was utilized to filter out low-quality data and perform
quality control. We excluded cells with gene expression counts lower
than 200 or higher than 2000. Additionally, cells with mitochondria
content exceeding 20% were discarded. A total of 19637 immune cells
were acquired for subsequent analysis. We normalized expression matrices
using NormalizeData functions. We then employed the FindVariable function
to identify the top 2000 variable genes and perform principal component
analysis (PCA) and then visualized using UMAP. We conducted cell type
annotation based on well-known marker genes, defining 6 major cell
types. The results were manually examined according to DEGs generated
by the FindMarkers function for each cell type.
Differential Expression Gene Analysis and Pathway Enrichment
Analysis
All DEG analyses were conducted using the FindMarkers
function within Seurat. The statistical approach utilized to identify
DEGs relied on the Wilcoxon Rank Sum test. The genes were defined
as differentially expressed with a log-fold-change threshold of 0.2.
The DEGs identified in each cluster or specific cell population (e.g.,
Lac.hi population) were conducted through pathway enrichment analysis
method, including GO and KEGG analysis using the ClusterProfiler R
package.
60
Preference Analysis
We identified the preference of
cell types in various samples employing the
R
o/e
index (
R
o/e
= Observed/Expected),
which was calculated as the observed ratio to expected cell numbers.
The actual counts were represented by the observed cell numbers, and
the expected cell numbers were analyzed by the chi-square test.
Cell–Cell Interaction Analysis
CellChat was
utilized to analyze ligand–receptor pairs among cell types.
We input gene expression data and cell type information into CellChat
and selected the “Secreted Signaling” human database
for subsequent analysis. Next, the ‘identifyOverExpressedGenes’
function was employed to infer overexpressed receptors and ligands
in specific cell groups, facilitating the construction of the cell–cell
communication network. The ‘min.cells’ parameter was
set to 10 to identify a strong signal pathway.
Trajectory Analysis
To infer the potential trajectory
in T cells, the R package Monocle was applied to reconstruct differentiation
hierarchies within the T cell clusters.
Statistical Analysis
The Kolmogorov–Smirnov
test was performed to analyze the statistical significance between
groups.
p
< 0.05 was considered as a statistical
difference. In all figures, ns,
p
> 0.05; *
p
< 0.05; **
p
< 0.01; ***
p
< 0.001; ****
p
< 0.0001.
body:
Introduction
Cancer is a systemic disease that is monitored
and eliminated by
the global immune system. The role of the tumor microenvironment has
been extensively studied, but the significant dynamic transformation
in the global immune landscape beyond tumors is increasingly recognized
as cancer progresses.
1
Peripheral blood
immune cells, crucial components of anticancer immunity, exhibit notable
changes during cancer progression and treatment. For instance, expanded
clonotypes found in the tumor and normal adjacent tissue can typically
be detected in peripheral T cells, as well. More importantly, previous
studies identified peripheral T cells that could predict prognosis
and clinical response.
2
Therefore, tracking
alterations in peripheral immune cells could serve as an effective
approach to detect cancers and predict immunotherapy response. However,
peripheral immune cell populations are heterogeneous, and their functional
states are multifaceted. Simply examining transcriptomics and the
T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire of T cells drew a partial picture,
given that immune cells are influenced by various factors, including
metabolic reprogramming, epigenetics, and post-translational modifications.
3
,
4
Among these, post-translational modifications, particularly glycosylation
on the cell surface, which was previously challenging to decode, are
now increasingly recognized for their significant role in influencing
the functional status of immune cells.
5
−
8
Glycan epitopes, while forming part
of cellular architecture, also
embody a rich tapestry of biological information.
9
−
11
They can serve
as the reporters for cell identities, owing to their sensitivity to
the physiological status.
12
,
13
It is noteworthy that
cell-surface glycans have been identified as active participants in
the regulation of immune signaling, and almost all key cell-surface
receptors in the immune system are glycoproteins.
5
,
6
Notably,
glycans are crucial for T cell development, signaling, and differentiation,
14
,
15
and have been validated as markers of distinct T cell functional
states in cancer,
16
,
17
underscoring their potential
as cancer biomarkers.
N
-acetyllactosamine (LacNAc),
a cell-surface glycan epitope, has been demonstrated as an indicator
of the glycolytic activity of T cells.
17
Besides, LacNAc treatment can restore the colocalization of TCR-CD8
or TCR-CD4 and effector activity of T cells.
7
,
8
However,
research into the role of LacNAc in immune cells has been cursory,
and past constraints in traditional technology have impeded the simultaneous
recognition and quantification of LacNAc levels.
18
Advanced single-cell glycomic multiomics could potentially
be the
game-changer in this field. Although conventional single-cell RNA
sequencing (scRNA-seq) revolutionized the understanding of the immune
cell populations in tumor immunology at the transcriptomic level,
19
−
21
other molecular modalities are still secrets and failed to demonstrate
the whole cell identity. Recent advances in single-cell multiomics
technologies are paving the way toward goals with various dimensions
of perspectives, including scTCR-, scBCR-, CITE-seq, Cellab-seq, and
so on.
22
−
25
For example, T-cell receptors (TCRs) play a crucial role in characterizing
the expansion of T cells due to recognizing the peptide-MHC complexes
(pMHC), thereby triggering the immune response.
26
scTCR-seq provides the sequence information on TCRs. To
advance the study of glycan epitopes in single-cell multiomics, we
are expanding upon the chemoenzymatic method for LacNAc detection.
27
,
28
We further reported that the platform in our previous research is
compatible with commercial single-cell platforms for detecting LacNAc
and can also integrate with other multiomics techniques.
17
Building on this foundation, we conducted
the study to comprehensively
analyze peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from bladder cancer
(BC) patients at various stages, focusing particularly on decoding
the information carried by the glycan epitope LacNAc on peripheral
blood immune cells, and we aim to improve our understanding of these
cells and potentially expand the applicability of “liquid biopsy”.
BC is one of the most prevalent genitourinary malignancies, with
its occurrence and mortality rates witnessing a recent rise.
29
Approximately 75% of BC patients present with
nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), which includes stages Ta
and T1.
30
A portion of NMIBC patients experience
progression to muscle-invasive or metastatic bladder cancer (MMIBC)
postsurgery, which includes stages T2–T4, often resulting in
a dire prognosis despite treatments like radical cystectomy and platinum-based
chemotherapy.
31
,
32
Effectively interpreting the
heterogeneity of immune cells in BC, particularly the differences
among BC at various stages, could provide precise insights into tumor
progression. We found that LacNAc levels on the surface of peripheral
blood immune cells decrease with the tumor stage progression. Therefore,
our approach could serve as a powerful tool for the large-scale detection
of surface glycans on peripheral blood immune cells.
2
,
33
In conclusion, LacNAc has been identified as a potential surface
marker of peripheral T cells in bladder cancer patients, providing
new insights into peripheral immune cell dynamics and opening avenues
for advancements in liquid biopsy techniques.
Results and Discussion
Working Principle and Study Design
Single-cell technologies
have propelled BC research forward at the transcriptomic,
34
spatial transcriptomic,
35
and epigenetic
36
levels, showcasing the
forces of single-cell omics. Recent advances also highlight the critical
role of glycosylation in diseases, particularly in cancer progression
and treatment.
9
However, research on the
specific glycan epitopes at the single-cell level is absent in BC
research.
In our prior research, identifying LacNAc molecules
on cellular surfaces was achieved using a chemoenzymatic approach,
which leverages the substrate flexibility of the recombinant
Helicobacter pylori
α1,3-fucosyltransferase
(1,3-FucT), allowing the transfer of fucose residue.
27
,
28
1,3-FucT selectively labels most glycan structures containing LacNAc
units, with varying efficiency across different LacNAc-containing
structures. From the perspective of substrate specificity,
N
-glycans with Neu5Ac or Neu5Gc linked to the α6 position
of Gal and
O
-glycans with polysaccharides (>disaccharides)
linked to the β6 position of GlcNAc were not recognized. Moreover,
although lectins can detect specific glycan structures containing
LacNAc units,
37
their recognition patterns
differ from the chemoenzymatic labeling of LacNAc. In summary, 1,3-FucT
allows the semiquantification of the LacNAc unit.
17
We have advanced this method by incorporating GDP-fucose
conjugated to single-stranded DNAs (GDP-Fucose-ssDNA,
Figure
1
), enhancing its applicability
to scRNA-seq. Similar to the foundational principles of scRNA-seq,
we have designed an ssDNA construct that includes a polymerase chain
reaction (PCR) handle, a barcode, and a poly(A) tail tailored for
the LacNAc library preparation. Once cells are lysed within their
microwells, magnetic beads capture both LacNAc and mRNA with poly(T)
tail sequences. After reverse transcription and amplification, the
library construction for RNA and LacNAc was concurrently finished.
This strategy is fully compatible with an established single-cell
platform, facilitating the integrated exploration of glycan epitopes
in cellular surfaces and single-cell multiomics
17
(workflow in
Figure
1
A).
Figure 1
Schematic diagram of the principle of sequencing and study design.
(A) An overview of the workflow for single-cell LacNAc-seq combined
with scRNA-seq and scTCR-seq. (B) The characteristics and the management
course of BC patients and the study design of experiment and analysis.
Using this method, we have quantified the LacNAc
level together
with transcriptomic and TCR data sets to profile the immune landscape
of PBMC from different stages of bladder cancer patients. Briefly,
6 PBMC samples were collected from 5 patients at different stages
of BC (
Table S1
), including one from whom
PBMC samples were obtained before/after anti-PD-1. The single-cell
suspension was obtained by sorting for CD45
+
cells via
flow cytometry (
Figures
1
B and
S1A
). As shown in
Figure S1B
, we successfully detected LacNAc labeling in PBMC
samples by using flow cytometry.
Distinct Single-Cell Immune Landscape of BC Patients
We initially utilized the shared barcode to integrate RNA, TCR, and
LacNAc data sets from all of the samples into a single Seurat object
for subsequent analysis, following the normalized data and stringent
quality control process, which included the filtration of doublets.
Through visualizing by uniform manifold approximation and projection
(UMAP), 19,637 immune cells were further clustered into 5 major cell
types, including T cell, NK cell, dendritic cell (DC), mononuclear
phagocytes (MPs), and B cell (
Figure
2
A,B). These specific cell types were defined by employing
well-established marker genes, leveraging their similar expression
patterns (
Figures
2
D,
S2, and S3
). The sample preference
of each cell type was illustrated using the
R
o/e
index (
Figure
2
C), which represents the ratio of observed to randomly expected
cell numbers, helping to account for technical variations in sample
preference estimation.
38
Intriguingly,
T cells and MPs are the predominant cellular populations in BC, accounting
for the majority of all cell types and displaying relatively even
distribution across the various samples (
Figures
2
A,C and
S4
). This
underscores the necessity for a more in-depth analysis of T cells
and MPs.
Figure 2
Single-cell landscape of CD45
+
immune cells in BC patients.
The UMAP plot showing the distribution of 19637 cells across main
cell types (A) and by sample (B). (C) Heatmap demonstrating the BC
stage and treatment preferences by the
R
o/e
score.
38
(D) The dot plot showing the
marker genes in different cell types. (E) The UMAP plot displaying
the LacNAc level. (F) The violin plot showing the LacNAc level in
various cell types (****
p
< 0.0001, Kolmogorov–Smirnov
test). (G) Overview of the LacNAc synthesis pathway. (H) GO analysis
revealing the pathway enrichment in Lac.hi (top 20%) vs Lac.low (bottom
20%). (I) Heatmap illustrating differentially expressed genes essential
for LacNAc biosynthesis between Lac.hi and Lac.low.
Single-Cell LacNAc Status of BC Patients
In parallel,
we quantified the LacNAc level and mapped it to its respective cells
on the UMAP plot based on the compatibility of the LacNAc procedure
with other omics approaches (
Figure
2
E). In BC patients, PBMCs demonstrated that significant
heterogeneity was observed in the level of LacNAc, with MPs and DC
displaying higher LacNAc levels, while T cells and NK cells exhibited
lower levels (
Figure
2
F). Subsequently, we selected cells ranked in the top 20% (Lac.hi)
and bottom 20% (Lac.low) according to LacNAc levels for differentially
expressed genes (DEGs) analysis. The Gene Ontology (GO) pathway analysis
enriched in Lac.hi is mainly associated with LacNAc-related synthesis
processes, such as the glycolytic process through fructose-6-phosphate
and the glycolytic process through glucose-6-phosphate (
Figure
2
G,H). As shown in
Figure
2
I, Lac.hi generally
expressed higher levels of key genes and enzymes that are crucial
for LacNAc biosynthesis, compared with Lac.low, including transcripts
described below: HK1–3 (encoding Hexokinase 1–3), ENO1
(encoding α-enolase), TPI1 (encoding Triosephosphate isomerase),
ADPGK (encoding ADP-dependent glucokinase), PFKL (encoding ATP-dependent
6-phosphofructokinase), PIGQ (encoding Phosphatidylinositol Glycan
Anchor Biosynthesis Class Q, GPI1), PKM (encoding Pyruvate kinase),
UAP1L1 (encoding UDP-
N
-acetylhexosamine pyrophosphorylase-like
protein 1), B3GNT2 (encoding β-1,3-
N
-Acetylglucosaminyltransferase
2), MGAT1 (encoding α-1,3-mannosyl-glycoprotein 2-β-
N
-acetylglucosaminyltransferase), and B4GALT1 (encoding
β-1,4-galactosyltransferase 1). These results strongly revealed
the capacity of single-cell omics to accurately reflect underlying
biological processes. More importantly, the activation of immune-related
processes could be related to high LacNAc levels (
Figure
2
H).
Heterogeneity in High and Low LacNAc Levels in Each Cell Type
To further discover the underlying variations between LacNAc levels
in different cell types, we compared Lac.hi and Lac.low cells within
each cell type. Interestingly, clear variances were observed in T
cells and MPs, whereas no obvious transcriptomic expression differences
could be detected in NK cells, B cells, and DCs (
Figure
3
A). Furthermore, Lac.hi T cells
were prominently associated with effector and cytotoxic phenotype
(e.g., GZMA, NKG7, IFNG), which will be discussed in detail subsequently.
In MPs, the expression of chemotaxis-related genes is notably elevated
in Lac.hi cells, such as CCL3, CCL4, CXCL2, etc. (
Figures
3
B and
S5
). As expected, GO and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes
(KEGG) pathway enrichment analyses indicated significant enrichment
in pathways related to chemotaxis and cytokine–cytokine receptor
interactions (
Figures
3
C and
S5
). These results collectively
suggest that T cells and MPs with high levels of LacNAc may play a
significant role in modulating the immune process in BC patients,
warranting further investigation to explore.
Figure 3
Evaluation of heterogeneity
between high and low LacNAc levels
in each cell type. (A) Heatmap showing transcriptional expression
difference between Lac.hi (top 20%) and Lac.low (bottom 20%) in different
cell types. (B) The volcano plot displaying the DEGs of Lac.hi and
Lac.low in MPs. (C) GO analysis revealing pathways that were enriched
in MPs with Lac.hi.
T cell Immune Landscape with LacNAc in BC Patients
Given the correlation between the high LacNAc level and T cell kill-related
genes in BC patients, along with the critical role of T cells in BC
progression and treatment, we further conducted a comprehensive single-cell
landscape of T cell gene expression. We subset T cells and further
annotated them as effector, naïve, and proliferative (prolif)
T cells based on functional gene markers (
Figures
4
A,C and
S6
). Notably,
the results showed that the LacNAc level of naïve T cells was
significantly lower than that of effector T cells and proliferative
T cells, which may be attributed to the quiescent state of naïve
T cells (
p
< 0.0001,
Figure
4
A,B). To further investigate the differences
between Lac.hi and Lac.low, we also utilized the top 20% and bottom
20% to decrypt the transcriptome characteristics (
Figure
4
D). Effector and prolif T cells
were mainly enriched in the Lac.hi group, while naïve T cells
constituted the majority in Lac.low (
Figure
4
E). At the transcriptomic level, we found
that genes associated with T cell activation and effector function
(such as FCER1G, CCL5, IFNG, GZMH, etc.) were upregulated in Lac.hi,
whereas genes indicative of immaturity (including CCR7, LEF1, and
SELL) were enriched in Lac.low (
Figure
4
F). Consistently, GO analysis revealed that the pathways
enriched in T cells with Lac.hi were predominantly associated with
T-cell-mediated immune cytotoxic activation and proliferation (
Figure
4
G).
Figure 4
T cells with high LacNAc
level in BC exhibit effector functional
phenotype at the (A) UMAP plot showing T cell subclusters and the
LacNAc level. (B) The violin plot demonstrating the LacNAc level on
different T cell types (****
p
< 0.0001, Kolmogorov–Smirnov
test). (C) The dot plot showing marker genes in different subclusters.
(D) The violin plot displaying the top, middle, and bottom group of
T cells according to the LacNAc level. Top 20%: Lac.hi. Bottom 20%:
Lac.low. (E) The stacked chart illustrating the distribution of T
cell types in Lac.hi and Lac.low. (F) The volcano plot displaying
the DEGs of Lac.hi and Lac.low in T cells. (G) GO analysis revealing
pathways that enriched in T cells with Lac.hi. (H) Circle plot showing
the inferred signaling networks between different cell types. (I)
Heatmap showing the T cell GSVA scores for glucose metabolism pathways.
(J) Differentially expressed genes essential for LacNAc biosynthesis
between Lac.hi and Lac.low in T cells.
DC and MPs are typically recognized as antigen-presenting
cells,
and their role in antigen presentation is essential for the activation
of T cells.
26
CellChat is a widely used
method for simulating intercellular communication, which predicts
the interaction strength between cell subpopulations based on scRNA-seq
39
Applying this method, we found that Lac.hi T
cells showed stronger interactions with MPs, whereas those with lower
levels of LacNAc did not, which could be one of the reasons for the
more potent effector phenotype of Lac.hi T cells (
Figure
4
H).
Because effector
T cells exhibit higher LacNAc levels compared
to naïve T cells, we were prompted to further investigate the
mechanisms regulating LacNAc levels in T cells. Given that glycan
biosynthesis is influenced by cellular metabolism,
40
we employed Gene Set Variation Analysis (GSVA),
41
a widely used method for assessing pathway activity
variation across a sample population, to calculate glycolysis pathway
activity scores. As anticipated, Lac.hi T cells exhibit higher GSVA
scores in various glucose metabolism pathways (
Figure
4
I) and demonstrate elevated expression levels
of key genes that are essential for LacNAc biosynthesis (
Figure
4
J).
LacNAc May be Negatively Correlated with Tumor Progression in
BC Patients
As the high-level LacNAc possesses potential
effectors and activation of T cells, we next investigated the relationship
between LacNAc and tumor progression. The UMAP plot illustrates the
distribution of samples across different stages (
Figure
5
A), while the
R
o/e
analysis reveals the sample preference of T cell subpopulations
(
Figure
5
B). We explored
our investigation according to the staging of disease in the samples.
Overall, LacNAc in NMIBC (<pT2) are significantly higher than those
in MIBC (≥pT2), suggesting that high LacNAc level T cells are
dramatically associated with the BC pathological tumor stage, namely,
LacNAc decreased as the tumor stage progressed (
p
< 0.0001,
Figure
5
C). To explore the underlying mechanism of the significance, we examined
the immune characteristics. LacNAc were found to have positive correlations
with effector biomarkers, including GZMA (
r
= 0.12,
p
= 5.17e-28), IFNG (
r
= 0.10,
p
= 3.60e-19), and NKG7 (
r
= 0.11,
p
= 4.96e-23) (
Figure
5
D), indicating that the T cells with high LacNAc levels
are significantly associated with cytotoxicity. This may explain why
tumors at lower stages tend to exhibit higher LacNAc levels.
Figure 5
LcNAc levels
may be correlated with tumor progression in BC patients.
(A) The UMAP plot showing the origins of T cells in BC patients. (B)
Heatmap demonstrating the BC stage and treatment preferences by the
R
o/e
score. (C) The violin plot displaying the
LacNAc level between NMIBC and MIBC (****
p
<
0.0001, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test). (D) Relationship between
the expression levels of LacNAc and GZMA, IFNG, NKG7 on T cells.
Taken together, these results strongly demonstrated
that T cells
with high LacNAc levels may serve as T cell activation markers in
BC patients.
LacNAc on T cell is Associated with T cell Differentiation State
and TCR Clonotype Expansion
As LacNAc is highly associated
with the effector functional phenotype, we further map the clonotype
expansion into the UMAP plot in combination with scTCR-seq (
Figure
6
A). Actually, the
clonal expansion of TCR has been widely identified as mediating tumor
cell cytotoxicity through TCR-pMHC interactions. In our scTCR-seq
results, patients at different stages generally showed a trend of
decreasing TCR clonal expansion with the progression of stages (
Figure
6
D). Additionally,
patient 1, undergoing combination therapy with anti-PD1, showed a
significant lesion reduction (
Figure S8
) and a notable increase in TCR clonotypes post-treatment (
Figure
6
D). Consistent with
what was identified above, we found that clonally expanded T cells
were notably more prevalent among Lac.hi T cells (
Figure
6
B). Moreover, T cells with
clonal expansion, encompassing expanded, medium, and small clone categories,
displayed significant differences in comparison to the single clone
group in the LacNAc level. Nonetheless, among T cells with clonal
expansion, no notable disparities were detected (
Figures
6
C and
S7A,B
). Through monocle-based pseudotime analysis, both LacNAc
levels and clone expansion were observed to progress from naive T
cells to those with effector phenotype capabilities (
Figure
6
E). These findings demonstrated
that T cells undergoing clonal expansion were observed to have a high
level of LacNAc.
Figure 6
LacNAc level on T cells may be associated with TCR clonotype
and
T cell differentiation states. (A) The UMAP plot showing the T cell
clonotype. (B) The stacked chart displaying the distribution of T
cell clonotype in Lac.hi and Lac.low. (C) The violin plot showing
the LacNAc level among different clonotype expansions (****
p
< 0.0001, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test). (D) Pie
charts showing the distribution of clonotypes of all T cells in each
patient based on clonal frequency. (E) Monocle-based pseudotime analysis
showing the differentiation trajectory, cell type, TCR clonotypes,
and the LacNAc level.
Summary
With the rapid advancement in glycobiology,
it becomes evident
that glycan epitopes are of great significance in a variety of biological
processes, such as signal transduction, immune responses, and cell
differentiation.
5
,
42
,
43
An in-depth exploration of their structure
44
and metabolic origins
45
has also been
explored. Although recent advancements in glycosylation position on
the cell surface directly demonstrate the potential value of glycans
in living cells,
46
−
48
the precise glycan recognition and quantitation of
immune cells in human tumor samples at single-cell resolution is still
lacking.
49
Our previous work has reported
a platform that can be integrated with existing single-cell technology,
enabling the quantification of cell-surface LacNAc at the single-cell
level. Herein, we first expanded our biochemical approaches
17
to PBMCs from human tumor patients, uncovering
intriguing phenomena related to glycobiology. These insights significantly
enhance our understanding of glycoimmunology.
The production
of glycan epitopes is a metabolic process. Recent
studies have highlighted a crucial connection between the metabolic
process of tumors and their progression.
45
,
50
,
51
Within the Lac.hi cell populations, we observed
pathway enrichment in glycolytic processes, including fructose-6-phosphate
and glucose-6-phosphate pathways. Other LacNAc-related genes, including
those involved in hexokinase pathways, UDP-GlcNAc biosynthesis, β-3-GlcNAc
transferases, and B4-Galtransferases, were found to be more highly
expressed in the Lac.hi cell population. This not only validates the
success of our technique but also offers a potential approach to exploring
cellular metabolism. More importantly, Lac.hi cell populations were
significantly enriched in lymphocyte-mediated immune regulation pathways,
fueling our enthusiasm to continue exploring according to cell types.
In MPs, we showed that the Lac.hi population is significantly enriched
in pathways related to chemokines. Chemokines profoundly reorganize
the tumor microenvironment.
52
Recent advances
have shown that chemokines in T-cell recruitment like CCL3, CCL4,
and CCL5 are associated with the presence of T cells in tumors.
53
,
54
Moreover, elevated secretion of chemokines by MPs, such as CCL5,
has been proven to recruit cytotoxic T cells for antitumor activity.
55
,
56
Taken together, MPs expressing high levels of LacNAc may recruit
more effector T cells through chemokines to exert the antitumor effect.
Subsequently, we further investigated the LacNAc characteristics
of peripheral T cells, finding that the Lac.hi T cell population exhibited
enrichment in effector T cell types, cytotoxic genes, and pathways.
Besides, we analyzed TCR clonotype expansion in BC patients from different
stages. As expected, NMIBC exhibits greater TCR clonal expansion than
those with MIBC, suggesting the stronger antitumor properties of T
cells. Notably, the T1 stage BC patient was treated with ICI. Our
scTCR-seq results indicated that post-treatment, there was a significant
increase in TCR clonal expansion, demonstrating the pronounced efficacy
of immunotherapy. Finally, we explored the potential relationship
between LacNAc and peripheral T-cell differentiation. Surprisingly,
LacNAc on peripheral T cells undergoes dynamic changes during the
differentiation process, and these changes are significantly associated
with the effector functions and clonotype expansion. In the early
work, researchers employed gal-binding lectins for glycan detection,
revealing that T cells undergo glycan remodeling following activation,
with a specific upregulation of terminal galactose structures.
57
,
58
Additionally, the peanut agglutinin high phenotype of activated
T cells results from the
de novo
synthesis of CD45
glycans.
58
In our study, we further advanced
glycan detection by employing single-cell glycomics sequencing technology
to analyze the surface glycans of immune cells derived from the PBMCs
of cancer patients. Our results confirmed that LacNAc is a potential
effector marker of T cells, and this mechanism may be linked to pathways
associated with glycolysis.
To our knowledge, our study is the
first to investigate the transcripts,
immune repertoires, and LacNAc mapping at the single-cell level in
the dynamic change of patient-derived immune cells. These findings
collectively indicate that the observed correlation between the LacNAc
level on peripheral T cells and T cell characteristics, including
TCR expanded clones and effector phenotypes, suggests that LacNAc
detection in peripheral T cells is a clinically potential tool. However,
there are still limitations in the current data. Although our data
show that LacNAc levels are higher in NMIBC compared to those in MIBC,
suggesting a potential negative correlation between LacNAc levels
and tumor progression, we were unable to obtain large-scale clinical
data with direct LacNAc measurements to accurately assess its prognostic
value. Although this approach holds clinical application prospects
and underscores the potential of this approach for liquid biopsy applications,
59
clinical cohorts with direct LacNAc measurements
are still needed to validate the association of LacNAc with prognosis,
immunotherapy efficacy.
In conclusion, we identified LacNAc
as a potential cell-surface
effector marker for peripheral T cells in BC patients. This discovery
enhances our understanding of peripheral immune cells and paves the
way for “liquid biopsy” advancements.
Method and Materials
Patients
This study included 5 BC patients at Nanjing
Drum Tower Hospital (Nanjing, China) from August 2015 to April 2022.
The pathological data of 5 patients with prognostic information are
recorded in
Table S1
. This study was approved
by the Ethics Committee of Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital (2021–394–01).
GDP-Fucose-ssDNA Synthesis and Labeling
The GDP-Fucose-ssDNA
synthesis process is consistent with our previous work.
17
In brief, GDP-Fucose-Am was produced from GDP-Fucose-Azide
using Pd/C in MeOH/ddH2O. GDP-Fucose-Am was then added to NaHCO
3
, THF, and NHS-PEG4-Tz (Click Chemistry Tools) to create GDP-Fucose-Am-Tz.
TCO-ssDNA was synthesized by reacting NH
2
-ssDNA (Sangon
Co., Ltd., Shanghai.) and NHS-PEG
4
-TCO (Xi’an Confluore
Biological Technology Co., Ltd.) in Borate Buffered Saline solution
with DMSO for 2 h at final concentrations of 200 μM and 8 mM,
respectively. TCO-ssDNA was purified using DNA adsorption columns
(Baiaolaibo Co., Ltd., Beijing). Finally, GDP-Fucose-Am-Tz and TCO-ssDNA
underwent a click reaction in a 1:1 ratio to synthesize GDP-Fucose-ssDNA.
To ensure compatibility with the Singleron platform, the probe was
designed as follows: TGTCAAGATGCTACCGTTCAGAGTAAGAGCCCGGCAAGAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA*A*A.
Cells were resuspended in 1× PBS containing 50 μg/mL
FucT, 20 mM Mg
2+
, 0.1 mg mL
–1
salmon
testes DNA, 0.1 μM Cy5-(dT)
25
, and 20 μM GDP-Fucose-ssDNA.
Following the completion of GDP-Fucose-ssDNA labeling, the detection
was carried out using an Agilent NovoCyte Quanteon flow cytometer.
Flow Cytometry
The PBMC fraction was isolated from
peripheral blood by Ficoll-Paque density gradient separation and then
prepared as single-cell suspensions, and Fc receptors were blocked
with Human TruStain FcX (Biolegend, 422302) before staining with fluorescent
antibodies. A Zombie Aqua Fixable Viability Kit was used to distinguish
live/dead cells (Biolegend, 423102). Alexa Flour700-antihuman-CD45
was used to identify immune cells, and the gating strategy is shown
in
Figure S1A
. The labeling of LacNAc (GDP-Fucose-ssDNA)
was tested with APC-poly(dT)-Cy5, as shown in
Figure S1B
.
Single-Cell Library Production
Single-cell suspensions
were captured using the microfluidic chip, and we used the Singleron
single-cell RNA-seq approach (GEXSCOPE Single-Cell RNA-seq Kit, Singleron
Biotechnologies, Nanjing, China), coupled with LacNAc-seq and scTCR-seq,
allowing for the simultaneous detection of the single-cell transcriptome,
LacNAc, and TCR clonotypes of PBMCs from bladder cancer patients.
Our group previously developed LacNAcTag ssDNA sequences, which can
be found in the previous article for details.
17
The poly(A) tail of mRNAs, TCR region, and LacNAc of cells were
captured by magnetic beads. In short, single-cell isolation, lysis,
reverse transcription, and complementary DNA (cDNA) amplification
were conducted based on the protocol. The construction of libraries
for mRNA, LacNAcTags, and TCR was carried out using Singleron RNA-seq
with feature barcoding and scTCR-seq protocols. Sequencing of the
libraries was conducted using the Illumina HiSeq X platform (Illumina).
Single-Cell Data Generation
Total reads from FASTQ
files were processed to generate gene expression matrices by the Singleron
platform CeleScope (
https://github.com/singleron-RD/CeleScope
). We filtered invalid reads and then extracted cell barcodes and
unique molecular identifiers (UMI). Prior to the mapping of reads
to GRCh38, reads with poly(A) tails were trimmed. Subsequently, we
grouped the same cell barcode, UMI, and gene to generate the number
of UMIs per gene per cell.
The analysis of LacNAcTags was also
performed using the Singleron platform CeleScope (multitag module)
for UMI counting. Normalized analysis of LacNAc was performed using
the following formula:
X
i
= log (
C
i
+ 1).
X
i
represented
log normalized data of the LacNAc and
C
i
represented the original UMI counts. The TCR repertoire data generated
from the flv_trust4 assay within CeleScope, the scRepertoire R package
was utilized for detailed analysis. The subsequent analysis was supported
by Seurat packages in R. The combination of the transcriptome, TCR,
and LacNAc was initially created into one Seurat object.
Quality Control and the Cell Type Annotation
The Seurat
package within R was utilized to filter out low-quality data and perform
quality control. We excluded cells with gene expression counts lower
than 200 or higher than 2000. Additionally, cells with mitochondria
content exceeding 20% were discarded. A total of 19637 immune cells
were acquired for subsequent analysis. We normalized expression matrices
using NormalizeData functions. We then employed the FindVariable function
to identify the top 2000 variable genes and perform principal component
analysis (PCA) and then visualized using UMAP. We conducted cell type
annotation based on well-known marker genes, defining 6 major cell
types. The results were manually examined according to DEGs generated
by the FindMarkers function for each cell type.
Differential Expression Gene Analysis and Pathway Enrichment
Analysis
All DEG analyses were conducted using the FindMarkers
function within Seurat. The statistical approach utilized to identify
DEGs relied on the Wilcoxon Rank Sum test. The genes were defined
as differentially expressed with a log-fold-change threshold of 0.2.
The DEGs identified in each cluster or specific cell population (e.g.,
Lac.hi population) were conducted through pathway enrichment analysis
method, including GO and KEGG analysis using the ClusterProfiler R
package.
60
Preference Analysis
We identified the preference of
cell types in various samples employing the
R
o/e
index (
R
o/e
= Observed/Expected),
which was calculated as the observed ratio to expected cell numbers.
The actual counts were represented by the observed cell numbers, and
the expected cell numbers were analyzed by the chi-square test.
Cell–Cell Interaction Analysis
CellChat was
utilized to analyze ligand–receptor pairs among cell types.
We input gene expression data and cell type information into CellChat
and selected the “Secreted Signaling” human database
for subsequent analysis. Next, the ‘identifyOverExpressedGenes’
function was employed to infer overexpressed receptors and ligands
in specific cell groups, facilitating the construction of the cell–cell
communication network. The ‘min.cells’ parameter was
set to 10 to identify a strong signal pathway.
Trajectory Analysis
To infer the potential trajectory
in T cells, the R package Monocle was applied to reconstruct differentiation
hierarchies within the T cell clusters.
Statistical Analysis
The Kolmogorov–Smirnov
test was performed to analyze the statistical significance between
groups.
